lesson.title: Town Meetings: Grassroots Democracy in Puritan New England
lesson.summary: Rooted in the self governing tradition of Puritan congregations, New England town meetings gave property owning colonists direct control over local decisions, becoming one of colonial America's most distinctive and enduring institutions of self government.
lesson.body:
Town meetings developed in New England almost from the moment Puritan settlers began establishing towns in the 1630s, and they grew naturally out of the religious practices these colonists already knew well. Puritan congregations were organized as self governing bodies, each individual church electing its own minister and managing its own affairs without oversight from bishops or a national hierarchy, since Puritans rejected the Church of England's centralized episcopal structure. When these same settlers organized civic life in their new towns, they applied a similar model: rather than deferring to a distant appointed authority, eligible townspeople gathered together to debate and vote on matters affecting their community directly.

At a typical town meeting, property owning men, often required to be church members in good standing during the earliest decades of Massachusetts Bay Colony, assembled to decide practical local matters: how to allocate town land, whether to build a new road or meetinghouse, how much to tax residents for shared expenses, and who should serve as selectmen, the small group of officials chosen to handle day to day town business between meetings. Dorchester, Massachusetts, is often credited with an early and influential version of this system, establishing in 1633 a group of twelve men chosen to manage town affairs, a practice widely seen as a forerunner of the selectmen system that spread throughout New England towns.

Town meetings gave ordinary colonists, at least those who met the property and often religious qualifications to participate, a level of direct influence over local government that was unusual for the seventeenth century, when most of the world remained governed by hereditary monarchs and distant elites. This tradition connected closely to the broader pattern of colonial governance across New England, where town meetings operated alongside colony wide assemblies, and it stood in meaningful contrast to the Southern Colonies, where large distances between plantations and government centered more on county courts dominated by planter elites made this kind of frequent, direct, local participation far less practical.

The town meeting tradition proved remarkably durable. It survived the political upheavals of the later colonial period and the Revolution, and many small New England towns continue to hold open town meetings to this day, making decisions on budgets and local ordinances through direct votes of assembled residents rather than through elected representatives alone. Nineteenth century observers, including the French writer Alexis de Tocqueville, later pointed to New England town meetings as an expression of the participatory, grassroots political culture that shaped American democracy more broadly, tracing a line from the small Puritan congregations of the 1630s to the wider American tradition of local self government.
